title: Remove a proven constant grouping key
note: Constant metadata allows the rule to remove a grouping key even without requiring a Project operand.
sql: SELECT city, k, COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT city, 1 AS k FROM customers) t GROUP BY city,k

title: Expand distinct aggregates using joins
note: Separate distinct inputs are aggregated and combined by a join.
sql: SELECT customer_id, COUNT(DISTINCT amount), SUM(DISTINCT id) FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id

title: Expand aggregation with distinct keys
note: WITHIN DISTINCT is expanded into grouped relational operators after SUM normalization. This example describes a plan; runtime uniqueness checks are not executed.
sql: SELECT customer_id,SUM(amount),SUM(amount) WITHIN DISTINCT (id) FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id

title: Move aggregation below a filter
note: Aggregation moves below the filter while retaining the columns needed to evaluate its predicate.
sql: SELECT city,COUNT(*) FROM customers WHERE id>10 GROUP BY city

title: Remove an unused nested outer join
note: Distinct aggregation makes an intermediate outer join redundant when its fields are not needed.
sql: SELECT DISTINCT c.name FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.id=o.customer_id LEFT JOIN orders p ON c.id=p.customer_id

title: Remove an outer join below distinct aggregation
note: Duplicate elimination on the preserved input makes the unused side of the outer join unnecessary.
sql: SELECT DISTINCT c.name FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.id=o.customer_id

title: Push partial aggregation below a join
note: Partial sums are placed on join inputs and combined above the join. No data is executed or performance gain measured.
sql: SELECT c.city,SUM(o.amount) FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.id=o.customer_id GROUP BY c.city

title: Combine nested aggregates
note: The upper SUM of counts is combined with the lower aggregation at the coarser grouping level.
sql: SELECT city, SUM(n) FROM (SELECT city,name,COUNT(*) n FROM customers GROUP BY city,name) t GROUP BY city

title: Remove a constant grouping key
note: The constant grouping key is pulled above the aggregate and restored in the output projection.
sql: SELECT city, k, COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT city, 1 AS k FROM customers) t GROUP BY city,k

title: Remove aggregation over unique literal rows
note: The literal input has distinct grouping keys, so MIN can be replaced by the corresponding input expression.
sql: SELECT id,MIN(id) FROM (VALUES (1),(2)) t(id) GROUP BY id

title: Remove redundant union-input aggregation
note: The outer distinct aggregate makes a duplicate-eliminating aggregate inside UNION ALL redundant.
sql: SELECT DISTINCT city FROM (SELECT DISTINCT city FROM customers UNION ALL SELECT DISTINCT city FROM customers) t

title: Remove aggregation from the first union input
note: The outer distinct aggregate makes the duplicate-eliminating aggregate in the first UNION ALL input redundant.
sql: SELECT DISTINCT city FROM (SELECT DISTINCT city FROM customers UNION ALL SELECT DISTINCT city FROM customers) t

title: Remove aggregation from the second union input
note: The outer distinct aggregate makes the duplicate-eliminating aggregate in the second UNION ALL input redundant.
sql: SELECT DISTINCT city FROM (SELECT DISTINCT city FROM customers UNION ALL SELECT DISTINCT city FROM customers) t

title: Evaluate aggregation over an empty input
note: Preparation exposes empty Values. The selected rule produces the aggregate result prescribed for empty input.
sql: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customers WHERE 1=0

title: Merge adjacent Calc programs
note: The filter and projection are first represented as separate Calc programs. The selected rule combines those programs.
sql: SELECT name FROM customers WHERE id>10

title: Lower decimal arithmetic in Calc
note: Decimal multiplication in a Calc program is rewritten using primitive numeric operations and scale adjustments.
sql: SELECT amount * 1.20 FROM orders

title: Fold a constant in Calc
note: After projection-to-Calc conversion, the multiplication in the expression program becomes a literal.
sql: SELECT name,10*20 AS threshold FROM customers

title: Remove an identity Calc
note: An identity projection is first represented as Calc. The selected rule removes that redundant program.
sql: SELECT * FROM customers

title: Split Calc into relational operators
note: The prepared Calc program is split into projection and filtering operators.
sql: SELECT name FROM customers WHERE id>10

title: Extract a window from Calc
note: The prepared Calc contains a window expression. The selected rule extracts it into a Window operator.
sql: SELECT name,ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY city ORDER BY id) rn FROM customers

title: Push a grouping-key predicate below aggregation
note: The HAVING condition references only a grouping key and can be evaluated before aggregation.
sql: SELECT city,COUNT(*) FROM customers GROUP BY city HAVING city='London'

title: Merge a filter into Calc
note: The input projection is first represented as Calc. The filter condition is then incorporated into that program.
sql: SELECT * FROM (SELECT id+1 AS id,name FROM customers) t WHERE id>10

title: Push a filter through Correlate
note: A join is first represented as Correlate. The selected rule moves eligible predicates to its inputs.
sql: SELECT c.name FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE o.amount>10

title: Push a filter into an inner join
note: The non-smart variant moves eligible predicates into the join inputs without applying the smart outer-join simplification.
sql: SELECT c.name FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE o.amount>100

title: Combine adjacent filters
note: Removing identity projections exposes two filters; the selected rule combines their predicates.
sql: SELECT * FROM (SELECT * FROM customers WHERE id>10) t WHERE id<20

title: Attach a filter to MultiJoin
note: The join tree is first represented as MultiJoin. The selected rule incorporates the filter into that representation.
sql: SELECT c.name FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE o.amount>10

title: Move a filter below sampling
note: The filter and sampling operators are reordered by the selected Calcite rule. Sample outcomes are not evaluated.
sql: SELECT * FROM customers TABLESAMPLE BERNOULLI(20) WHERE id>10

title: Push a filter into set-operation inputs
note: The same predicate is evaluated on the inputs of UNION ALL.
sql: SELECT * FROM (SELECT id,name FROM customers UNION ALL SELECT id,name FROM customers) t WHERE id>10

title: Expand a filter subquery
note: SQL conversion preserves the IN subquery so that the selected rule can produce its relational rewrite.
sql: SELECT name FROM customers WHERE id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders)

title: Push a partition-key filter below Window
note: Window extraction and filter transposition expose the Window. The city predicate keeps whole partitions and can move below it.
sql: SELECT * FROM (SELECT id,city,ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY city ORDER BY id) rn FROM customers) t WHERE city='London'

title: Rebuild joins from a hypergraph
note: After hypergraph construction, Calcite’s experimental join reordering rule produces a join tree. Estimates use schema-only metadata.
sql: SELECT c.name FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.id=o.customer_id JOIN orders p ON c.id=p.customer_id

title: Flatten nested intersections
note: Nested intersections are combined into a single set operation with more inputs.
sql: (SELECT name FROM customers INTERSECT SELECT city FROM customers) INTERSECT SELECT name FROM customers

title: Introduce a redundant semijoin
note: An additional semijoin is introduced as an optimizer candidate. The demonstration stops after one match and does not claim a cheaper plan.
sql: SELECT c.name FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id

title: Regroup a three-input join
note: The left-nested join is rewritten as a right-nested join with adjusted predicates. One match is shown.
sql: SELECT c.name FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.id=o.customer_id JOIN orders p ON c.id=p.customer_id

title: Swap inner-join inputs
note: The join inputs are swapped and a projection preserves the original output order. A one-match limit prevents repeated swaps.
sql: SELECT c.name FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id

title: Swap join inputs with the outer-capable variant
note: This variant permits outer joins as well as inner joins. The bounded example shows one input swap and preserves output order.
sql: SELECT c.name FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id

title: Infer non-null join inputs
note: Equality in an inner join allows non-null predicates to be inferred for nullable join keys.
sql: SELECT c.name FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id

title: Distribute a join over its left union input
note: The join is applied to each UNION ALL branch on the left.
sql: SELECT c.name FROM (SELECT * FROM customers UNION ALL SELECT * FROM customers) c JOIN orders o ON c.id=o.customer_id

title: Use a semijoin with a unique right input
note: The right literal keys are unique and only left-side fields are projected, allowing a semijoin rewrite.
sql: SELECT c.name FROM customers c JOIN (VALUES (1),(2)) v(id) ON c.id=v.id

title: Pull both input projections above a join
note: Computed join-input projections are pulled above the inner join, with field references rewritten to preserve the result.
sql: SELECT c.name FROM (SELECT id+1 AS id,name FROM customers) c INNER JOIN (SELECT customer_id+1 AS customer_id,amount FROM orders) o ON c.id=o.customer_id

title: Pull both input projections above a join
note: Computed join-input projections are pulled above the outer join, with field references rewritten to preserve the result.
sql: SELECT c.name FROM (SELECT id+1 AS id,name FROM customers) c LEFT JOIN (SELECT customer_id+1 AS customer_id,amount FROM orders) o ON c.id=o.customer_id

title: Pull left input projections above a join
note: Computed join-input projections are pulled above the inner join, with field references rewritten to preserve the result.
sql: SELECT c.name FROM (SELECT id+1 AS id,name FROM customers) c INNER JOIN orders o ON c.id=o.customer_id

title: Pull left input projections above a join
note: Computed join-input projections are pulled above the outer join, with field references rewritten to preserve the result.
sql: SELECT c.name FROM (SELECT id+1 AS id,name FROM customers) c LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.id=o.customer_id

title: Pull right input projections above a join
note: Computed join-input projections are pulled above the inner join, with field references rewritten to preserve the result.
sql: SELECT c.name FROM customers c INNER JOIN (SELECT customer_id+1 AS customer_id,amount FROM orders) o ON c.id=o.customer_id

title: Pull right input projections above a join
note: Computed join-input projections are pulled above the outer join, with field references rewritten to preserve the result.
sql: SELECT c.name FROM customers c LEFT JOIN (SELECT customer_id+1 AS customer_id,amount FROM orders) o ON c.id=o.customer_id

title: Infer a predicate across an equality join
note: A range predicate on one order input is propagated to the other input through equality of their nullable customer IDs.
sql: SELECT a.id FROM (SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id > 10) a JOIN orders b ON a.customer_id = b.customer_id

title: Distribute a join over its right union input
note: The join is applied to each UNION ALL branch on the right.
sql: SELECT c.name FROM customers c JOIN (SELECT * FROM orders UNION ALL SELECT * FROM orders) o ON c.id=o.customer_id

title: Expand a subquery in a join condition
note: SQL conversion preserves the aggregate subquery in the join condition for the selected rule to rewrite.
sql: SELECT c.name FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.id=o.customer_id AND o.amount > (SELECT AVG(amount) FROM orders)

title: Represent joins as a hypergraph
note: The join tree becomes Calcite’s experimental HyperGraph representation.
sql: SELECT c.name FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.id=o.customer_id JOIN orders p ON c.id=p.customer_id

title: Flatten a join tree into MultiJoin
note: The binary join tree becomes a MultiJoin representation for subsequent join-order rules.
sql: SELECT c.name FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.id=o.customer_id JOIN orders p ON c.id=p.customer_id

title: Combine nested fetch limits
note: Removing identity projections exposes two fetch operators, which are combined into the tighter limit.
sql: SELECT * FROM (SELECT * FROM customers FETCH NEXT 10 ROWS ONLY) t FETCH NEXT 5 ROWS ONLY

title: Flatten a nested set difference
note: A left-nested EXCEPT is flattened while preserving the order of the subtracted inputs.
sql: (SELECT name FROM customers EXCEPT SELECT city FROM customers) EXCEPT SELECT name FROM customers

title: Choose a join tree from MultiJoin
note: After flattening and recording projected fields, the rule constructs a join tree using Calcite’s heuristic ordering.
sql: SELECT c.name FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.id=o.customer_id JOIN orders p ON c.id=p.customer_id

title: Construct a bushy join tree
note: The prepared MultiJoin is converted into a potentially bushy join tree. No real statistics or runtime cost measurements are supplied.
sql: SELECT c.name FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.id=o.customer_id JOIN orders p ON c.id=p.customer_id

title: Remove unused aggregate calls
note: The outer projection does not use COUNT, allowing the aggregate call to be removed while retaining grouping.
sql: SELECT city FROM (SELECT city,COUNT(*) n FROM customers GROUP BY city) t

title: Merge a projection into Calc
note: The filter is first converted to Calc. The output projection is then incorporated into that program.
sql: SELECT name FROM customers WHERE id>10

title: Prune Correlate input columns
note: A join is first represented as Correlate. Projections retain output columns and required correlation fields.
sql: SELECT c.name FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id

title: Push whole expressions below a filter
note: Both projection and predicate expressions are considered as whole expressions during transposition.
sql: SELECT id+1 FROM customers WHERE id*2>10

title: Push whole projection expressions below a filter
note: The computed output expression moves below Filter, with fields needed by the predicate retained.
sql: SELECT id+1 FROM customers WHERE id*2>10

title: Evaluate a projection and filter on literal rows
note: Filtering and projection are evaluated over Values and replaced with the resulting literal rows.
sql: SELECT id+1 FROM (VALUES (1),(2),(3)) t(id) WHERE id>1

title: Remove a redundant nested outer join
note: The first outer join has a unique right key and contributes no requested fields, allowing it to be removed.
sql: SELECT c.id,p.customer_id FROM customers c LEFT JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT customer_id FROM orders) o ON c.id=o.customer_id LEFT JOIN orders p ON c.id=p.customer_id

title: Remove an unused outer join
note: The right input is unique on the join key and no right-side field is projected, allowing the outer join to be removed.
sql: SELECT c.name FROM customers c LEFT JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT customer_id FROM orders) o ON c.id=o.customer_id

title: Combine adjacent projections
note: Preparation moves a projection through a filter and back, exposing adjacent projections for the selected rule to merge.
sql: SELECT name FROM customers WHERE id>10

title: Record requested fields in MultiJoin
note: The join tree is flattened first. The projection then records which MultiJoin fields are required.
sql: SELECT c.name FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.id=o.customer_id JOIN orders p ON c.id=p.customer_id

title: Normalize a windowed SUM
note: The windowed SUM is expressed using SUM0 and the expressions needed to preserve NULL semantics.
sql: SELECT SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY id) FROM orders

title: Prune columns before a set operation
note: The projection moves into UNION ALL inputs so they retain only the requested fields.
sql: SELECT name FROM (SELECT * FROM customers UNION ALL SELECT * FROM customers) t

title: Expand a scalar projection subquery
note: SQL conversion preserves subqueries for this example. The selected rule replaces the scalar subquery with relational operators and correlation.
sql: SELECT name, (SELECT MAX(amount) FROM orders WHERE customer_id=c.id) AS total FROM customers c

title: Extract a window operator
note: ROW_NUMBER moves from a projection expression into an explicit Window operator.
sql: SELECT name,ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY city ORDER BY id) rn FROM customers

title: Replace a join and distinct input with a semijoin
note: Only customer fields are projected, so the join to distinct customer IDs can become a semijoin.
sql: SELECT c.name FROM customers c JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT customer_id FROM orders) o ON c.id=o.customer_id

title: Prune unused Window input columns
note: After window extraction, the selected rule removes input columns that the window and output do not need.
sql: SELECT rn FROM (SELECT name,ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY city ORDER BY id) rn FROM customers) t

title: Represent Bernoulli sampling as a filter
note: The Bernoulli sample becomes a filter using a random predicate.
sql: SELECT * FROM customers TABLESAMPLE BERNOULLI(20)

title: Push a semijoin through a filter
note: A distinct-input join is first converted to a semijoin. The selected rule moves that semijoin below the filter.
sql: SELECT c.name FROM (SELECT * FROM customers WHERE id>10) c JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT customer_id FROM orders) o ON c.id=o.customer_id

title: Push a semijoin into a join input
note: The semijoin is prepared first, then moved into the side of the underlying join that supplies its keys.
sql: SELECT c.name FROM customers c JOIN orders p ON c.id=p.customer_id JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT customer_id FROM orders) o ON c.id=o.customer_id

title: Push a semijoin through a projection
note: The selected rule rewrites semijoin keys through the prepared input projection.
sql: SELECT c.name FROM (SELECT id+1 AS id,name FROM customers) c JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT customer_id FROM orders) o ON c.id=o.customer_id

title: Remove a redundant semijoin candidate
note: Preparation adds a redundant semijoin. The selected rule removes it; this is not a general claim that arbitrary semijoins are unnecessary.
sql: SELECT c.name FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id

title: Copy sort keys below a join
note: The selected rule copies applicable ordering keys into join inputs while keeping the original sort.
sql: SELECT c.name FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY c.name FETCH NEXT 5 ROWS ONLY

title: Push top-N through an outer join
note: The ordering refers to the preserved left input, allowing a sort bound to move below the outer join.
sql: SELECT * FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.id=o.customer_id ORDER BY c.name FETCH NEXT 5 ROWS ONLY

title: Remove a constant sort key
note: The filter proves the ordering key is constant, making that key unnecessary for sorting.
sql: SELECT * FROM customers WHERE id=1 ORDER BY id

title: Remove sorting on a one-row result
note: The global aggregate returns at most one row, making the sort and larger fetch bound redundant.
sql: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customers ORDER BY 1 FETCH NEXT 10 ROWS ONLY

title: Push a top-N bound into union inputs
note: After identity projection removal, sorts with fetch bounds are copied into UNION ALL inputs while the top sort is retained.
sql: SELECT name FROM customers UNION ALL SELECT city FROM customers ORDER BY 1 FETCH NEXT 5 ROWS ONLY

title: Push sorting into union inputs
note: This variant also accepts sorts without fetch. The example shows top-N sorts on UNION ALL inputs.
sql: SELECT name FROM customers UNION ALL SELECT city FROM customers ORDER BY 1 FETCH NEXT 5 ROWS ONLY

title: Flatten nested unions
note: Nested unions with compatible duplicate semantics are combined into one Union.
sql: (SELECT name FROM customers UNION SELECT city FROM customers) UNION SELECT name FROM customers

title: Pull a shared constant above a union
note: A constant output shared by both union branches is restored by a projection above the union.
sql: SELECT name,1 AS k FROM customers UNION ALL SELECT city,1 AS k FROM customers

title: Combine literal set-operation inputs
note: After removing identity projections, the union of literal rows is folded into Values with duplicate elimination.
sql: SELECT * FROM (VALUES (1),(2)) t(id) UNION SELECT * FROM (VALUES (2),(3)) t(id)

title: Simplify expressions in a Window
note: After window extraction, the selected rule reduces expressions associated with the window program.
sql: SELECT SUM(10*20) OVER (PARTITION BY city) FROM customers

title: Rewrite date extraction as a range
note: With the planner configured for UTC, year and month predicates are rewritten into timestamp ranges.
sql: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE EXTRACT(YEAR FROM created_at)=2025 AND EXTRACT(MONTH FROM created_at)=6

title: Prune empty input in aggregate
note: Preparation proves an input empty. The selected pruning rule rewrites the aggregate operation while preserving its empty-input and outer-join semantics.
sql: SELECT city,COUNT(*) FROM customers WHERE 1=0 GROUP BY city

title: Prune empty input in correlate left
note: Preparation proves an input empty. The selected pruning rule rewrites the correlate left operation while preserving its empty-input and outer-join semantics.
sql: SELECT * FROM (SELECT * FROM customers WHERE 1=0) c JOIN orders o ON c.id=o.customer_id

title: Prune empty input in correlate right
note: Preparation proves an input empty. The selected pruning rule rewrites the correlate right operation while preserving its empty-input and outer-join semantics.
sql: SELECT * FROM orders o LEFT JOIN (SELECT * FROM customers WHERE 1=0) c ON c.id=o.customer_id

title: Prune empty input in filter
note: Preparation proves an input empty. The selected pruning rule rewrites the filter operation while preserving its empty-input and outer-join semantics.
sql: SELECT * FROM (SELECT * FROM customers FETCH NEXT 0 ROWS ONLY) t WHERE id>10

title: Prune empty input in intersect
note: Preparation proves an input empty. The selected pruning rule rewrites the intersect operation while preserving its empty-input and outer-join semantics.
sql: (SELECT * FROM customers WHERE 1=0) INTERSECT SELECT * FROM customers

title: Prune empty input in join left
note: Preparation proves an input empty. The selected pruning rule rewrites the join left operation while preserving its empty-input and outer-join semantics.
sql: SELECT * FROM (SELECT * FROM customers WHERE 1=0) c JOIN orders o ON c.id=o.customer_id

title: Prune empty input in join right
note: Preparation proves an input empty. The selected pruning rule rewrites the join right operation while preserving its empty-input and outer-join semantics.
sql: SELECT * FROM orders o LEFT JOIN (SELECT * FROM customers WHERE 1=0) c ON c.id=o.customer_id

title: Prune empty input in minus
note: Preparation proves an input empty. The selected pruning rule rewrites the minus operation while preserving its empty-input and outer-join semantics.
sql: (SELECT * FROM customers WHERE 1=0) EXCEPT SELECT * FROM customers

title: Prune empty input in project
note: Preparation proves an input empty. The selected pruning rule rewrites the project operation while preserving its empty-input and outer-join semantics.
sql: SELECT * FROM customers WHERE 1=0

title: Prune empty input in sort
note: Preparation proves an input empty. The selected pruning rule rewrites the sort operation while preserving its empty-input and outer-join semantics.
sql: SELECT * FROM customers WHERE 1=0 ORDER BY id

title: Prune empty input in union
note: Preparation proves an input empty. The selected pruning rule rewrites the union operation while preserving its empty-input and outer-join semantics.
sql: (SELECT * FROM customers WHERE 1=0) UNION ALL SELECT * FROM customers

title: Simplify a projected single-row input
note: The projected one-row Values input on the left is absorbed into equivalent expressions and predicates.
sql: SELECT c.name FROM (SELECT 1+1 AS id) v JOIN customers c ON v.id=c.id

title: Simplify a join with one literal row
note: A one-row Values input on the right is replaced with equivalent expressions and predicates.
sql: SELECT c.name FROM customers c JOIN (VALUES (1)) v(id) ON c.id=v.id

title: Simplify a projected single-row input
note: The projected one-row Values input on the right is absorbed into equivalent expressions and predicates.
sql: SELECT c.name FROM customers c JOIN (SELECT 1+1 AS id) v ON c.id=v.id
